items.title: Lesson 2, Focus Question: A hardware store must choose between a plane mirror and a convex mirror for the end of a busy aisle. What are the advantages and disadvantages of the convex mirror?

body.html: Compare what each mirror does to image size, field of view, and clarity.

answer.html: Advantages: a convex mirror gives a much wider field of view, so a clerk can see the whole aisle (and shoppers around the corner) in one small mirror; it always produces an upright image. Disadvantages: the images are reduced and distances are distorted (objects look smaller and farther away than they are), and a spherical convex mirror also has some spherical aberration. A plane mirror gives an undistorted, same-size, upright image but a much narrower field of view.

items.title: Lesson 2, Get It?: What does it mean if |𝑚| > 1 for an image formed by a mirror?

body.html: 𝑚= ℎ<sub>𝑖</sub>/ ℎ<sub>𝑜</sub> compares the image size with the object size.

answer.html: If the magnitude of 𝑚 is greater than 1, the image is larger than the object (enlarged). A positive 𝑚 means it is also upright (virtual); a negative 𝑚 means it is inverted (real). For example, 𝑚= −2.5 is a real, inverted image 2.5 times as tall as the object.

items.title: Lesson 2, Figure 13 prompt: A concave mirror forms an image of an arrow standing on the principal axis. The tip of the image has been found with two rays. Explain how to locate the image of the arrow's base and of a point one-quarter of the way up the arrow.

body.html: Every point of the object sends out its own rays, and each object point forms its own image point.

A point on the principal axis (the base of the arrow) sends a ray along the axis. It reflects straight back on itself, so the image of the base is also on the axis, directly below the image tip. For the point one-quarter of the way up, draw its parallel ray (reflects through F) and its focal ray (through F, reflects parallel). They cross at a point one-quarter of the way up the image arrow.

answer.html: Repeat the two-ray construction for each object point (or use the base's ray along the axis); the image points form a straight arrow that runs from the axis to the image tip, and the point one- quarter up the object maps to the point one-quarter up the image.

Only a concave mirror used with the object closer than the focal length (0 < 𝑥<sub>𝑜</sub>< 𝑓) gives an enlarged, upright (virtual) image. A plane mirror gives 𝑚= 1 and a convex mirror gives 𝑚< 1.
Sketch: a small concave mirror on a handle held a centimeter or two from the tooth; the reflected rays diverge, and their sight lines meet behind the mirror in a larger upright image.

answer.html: Use a small concave mirror, with the tooth between the mirror and its focal point; it gives an enlarged, upright, virtual image (𝑥<sub>𝑖</sub>= −3.0 cm, 𝑚= + 2.0).

items.title: Lesson 2, Figure 14 prompt: In a concave shaving mirror, your face looks large and upright, but the window behind you looks small and upside down. What causes the other images?

body.html: Your face is inside the focal point, so it gives an upright, virtual image. The window is far beyond 2𝑓, so the mirror forms a real, inverted, reduced image of it in front of the mirror.

answer.html: The face (inside 𝑓) gives an upright virtual image behind the mirror, while the window (far beyond 2𝑓) forms a real, inverted, reduced image between 𝑓 and 2𝑓 in front of the mirror, which is why it appears upside down.

items.title: Lesson 2, Get It?: How can you tell, without calculating, whether a mirror image is real?

answer.html: A real image is formed where reflected rays actually cross, so it is in front of the mirror (𝑥<sub>𝑖</sub>> 0) and can be projected on a screen placed there; it is inverted. A virtual image is formed only where sight lines appear to meet behind the mirror (𝑥<sub>𝑖</sub>< 0), cannot be projected, and is always upright. So test: hold a card at the image position; if the image appears on the card, it is real.

items.title: Lesson 2, Figure 16 prompt: A convex mirror at the corner of a parking garage shows approaching cars looking small and far away. Why is that a safety problem, and how can a label help?

answer.html: A convex mirror forms reduced images, and a smaller image looks farther away. A driver who judges distance by apparent size would think a car is farther away than it really is and might pull out too soon. A label such as "objects are closer than they appear" reminds the driver to allow extra room.

items.title: Lesson 2, Get It?: Why do large telescopes and satellite dishes use parabolic reflectors rather than spherical ones?

answer.html: A sphere reflects parallel rays that hit far from the axis to a point nearer the mirror than rays that hit close to the axis, so the rays do not meet at one focal point (spherical aberration, a blurry image). A parabola has exactly the shape that sends every ray parallel to its axis through the single focal point, whatever its distance from the axis, so the focus is sharp.

items.title: Lesson 2, Check Your Progress 29: Two spherical mirrors have the same radius of curvature, 2.0 m. Mirror A is 5 cm wide; mirror B is 80 cm wide. Which gives the sharper focus of distant starlight, and why?

body.html: The mirror equation, and a single focal point, assume the paraxial approximation: only rays close to the principal axis.

answer.html: Mirror A gives the sharper focus. Its height is small compared with its radius of curvature, so every ray strikes close to the axis, where a sphere is almost identical to a parabola, and the reflected rays all pass very nearly through the same focal point. Mirror B reflects rays that strike far from the axis to a point closer to the mirror, so its image is blurred by spherical aberration.

items.title: Lesson 2, Focus Question: Advantages and disadvantages of curved mirrors compared with plane mirrors

body.html: Compare what each mirror does to the image size, field of view, and clarity.

answer.html: Advantages: a concave mirror can magnify (object inside 𝑓), form real images that can be projected, and focus parallel light to a point (telescopes, headlights, solar collectors); a convex mirror gives a much wider field of view (store security mirrors, passenger-side mirrors). Disadvantages: the images are not life-size and distances are distorted (convex images look smaller and farther away; concave images can be inverted), and spherical mirrors suffer spherical aberration (fuzzy images). A plane mirror gives an undistorted, same-size, upright image.

items.title: Lesson 2, Get It?: How can you determine whether an image is virtual?

answer.html: A virtual image is formed only where the sight lines (extended rays) appear to meet, not where actual light rays cross. It is on the opposite side of the mirror from the object (𝑥<sub>𝑖</sub>< 0), is always upright, and cannot be projected on a screen. items.title: Lesson 2, Check Your Progress 29: Spherical aberration and mirror height

body.html: The mirror equation (and a single focal point) assumes the paraxial approximation: only rays close to the principal axis.

answer.html: The aberration is smaller for a mirror whose height is small compared with its radius of curvature. Then every ray strikes close to the axis, where a sphere is almost identical to a parabola, so the reflected rays all pass very nearly through the same focal point.
